name: 118e06 · MLII · 09:05.0–09:15.0

comments: Created by `nst' from records 118 and em (SNR = 6 dB)

alignment.metric_alignment: DC-invariant: each signal's mean is removed before error metrics
alignment.display_alignment: plots align each trace to the reference mean

notes: 129-tap Type I linear-phase FIR (Hamming window). Applied with forward-backward zero-phase filtering.
Causal group delay would be 64.0 samples (177.78 ms); it is cancelled by zero-phase filtering.
Order-4 Butterworth IIR (4 second-order sections), applied with forward-backward zero-phase filtering.
IIR phase delay is frequency-dependent and is cancelled by zero-phase filtering.

warnings: A constant DC offset of -7.965 mV was removed from the NSTDB record before filtering and metric calculation.
conclusions: Input SNR on this segment is -10.82 dB. FIR improves it by +2.47 dB (to -8.35 dB); IIR improves it by +0.70 dB (to -10.13 dB).
FIR has the lower residual RMSE (1.0889 mV vs 1.3359 mV).
FIR provides the larger SNR gain for this noise/filter combination.
FIR preserves the annotated-beat morphology windows better on average (mean correlation 0.631 vs 0.569).
FIR was faster in this run (1.64 ms vs 4.72 ms, design + filtering, median of three filter passes).

Linear decomposition: FIR suppresses additive noise by 2.41 dB with 0.0824 mV RMS signal distortion; IIR suppresses it by 0.81 dB with 0.2033 mV distortion. Total SNR and morphology metrics reflect this trade-off.

The NSTDB nominal SNR for this record is +6 dB, but nst defines it from QRS amplitude and frequency-weighted noise, not conventional power SNR. Compare the measured value above rather than treating them as identical.
No universal winner is claimed: the better choice depends on the noise band, the allowed filter order, edge effects and the need to preserve specific waveforms.
